content: 1. In April and September 1993, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) organized two advisory workshops to evaluate and update recommendations regarding water fluoridation practices. 2. Since 1979, the CDC has developed guidelines and recommendations specifically for managers of public water systems that utilize fluoridation. 3. This report consolidates and updates the CDC's previous recommendations while summarizing the outcomes of the two workshops. 4. 5. The report provides detailed recommendations concerning the engineering aspects of water fluoridation, including administration, monitoring, surveillance, technical requirements, and safety protocols. 6. These recommendations address water fluoridation for both community public water supply systems and school public water supply systems. 7. Water fluoridation involves the intentional addition of fluoride, a natural trace element, to drinking water in accordance with established scientific and dental guidelines. 8. Fluoride is naturally present in varying amounts in soil, water supplies, plants, and animals, making it a normal component of all diets. 9. In mammals, the highest concentrations of fluoride are found in bones and teeth. 10. Since 1945, numerous studies have demonstrated the oral health benefits of fluoride and water fluoridation. 11. 12. Research consistently indicates that fluoridation is safe and represents the most cost-effective and practical method for reducing the incidence of dental caries in communities. 13. However, additional studies have shown that the oral health benefits of fluoridation are diminished if optimal fluoride levels are not maintained. 14. Historically, maintaining optimal fluoride levels without active monitoring and surveillance programs has been challenging. 15. In the 1970s, approximately half of the systems presumed to be fluoridated were not consistently maintaining optimal fluoride concentrations. 16. Since the late 1970s, the CDC has developed technical and administrative guidelines to address inconsistencies in fluoridated public water supply systems. 17. In April and September 1993, the CDC convened two advisory workshops to review and revise fluoridation guidelines, with participation from 11 technical experts from state agencies and the Indian Health Service. 18. Additional input was obtained from state dental officials, state drinking water personnel, and other stakeholders, including public health schools, dental societies, and private industry engineers. 19. The intent of these recommendations is to provide guidance to federal, state, and local officials involved in the engineering or administrative aspects of water fluoridation, ensuring that fluoridated water systems deliver optimal fluoride levels. 20. This report consolidates information from earlier studies linking fluoridation to reduced dental caries, summarizes the conclusions of the workshops, provides recommendations for fluoridation of community and school public water supplies, and updates previous recommendations. 21. These recommendations are written with the assumption that the reader has either an engineering background or familiarity with basic water supply engineering principles. 22. A glossary of technical terms is included to assist readers. 23. The preventive effects of waterborne fluoride on tooth decay were first recognized in the early 1900s in Colorado Springs, Colorado, when a dentist observed tooth discoloration, later termed Colorado Brown Stain (now known as fluorosis), in many of his patients. 24. Research revealed that fluorosis was prevalent in the surrounding El Paso County and was associated with fluoride in the water. It was also noted that individuals with fluorosis had significantly fewer dental caries. 25. Subsequent studies confirmed the cause-and-effect relationship between fluoridation and the reduction of dental caries. 26. Public water systems, regardless of ownership, must meet specific criteria to be classified as public water systems, including serving at least 15 service connections or regularly serving an average of at least 25 people for at least 60 days per year. 27. Public water systems do not necessarily align with city, county, or state boundaries, and individual states have varying regulations and guidelines for water systems. 28. Schools with individual water systems are considered public water systems and are subject to the same rules, though they are categorized as nontransient, noncommunity public water systems due to their limited use and size. 29. Special recommendations and guidelines for school public water systems are included in this report. 30. Although no national regulations govern water fluoridation, many federal agencies agree on its public health benefits. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has established national requirements for public water systems but not for adjusted water fluoridation. 31. The EPA has set a maximum concentration level for natural fluoride in drinking water, and any excess must be removed. 32. Recommendations for fluoridated community public water supply systems include detailed guidelines for administration, monitoring, technical requirements, and safety procedures. 33. 34. 35. Technical requirements for fluoridation systems include interlocking feed systems, proper injection points, and the use of anti-siphon devices to prevent overfeeds. 36. 37. 38. School water fluoridation is recommended only for schools with independent water sources, and state-level resources must be available to support operational and maintenance responsibilities. 39. 40. Technical requirements for school water fluoridation systems align with those for community systems, with additional considerations for the unique needs of schools.
